❯ Without using any tools, write about 350 words explaining how a terminal emulator turns a
  byte stream into a cell grid. Use a couple of short paragraphs and a short bulleted list.

● A terminal emulator sits between a program writing bytes to a pseudoterminal and a window
  showing characters. Its job is to consume that byte stream — which carries no structure
  beyond the bytes themselves — and maintain a two-dimensional array of cells, each holding a
  character (or grapheme cluster), a foreground and background color, and attribute flags
  like bold, italic, or underline. Everything the user sees is a render of that array.

  The first stage is decoding. Bytes arrive in arbitrary chunks, so a UTF-8 decoder must hold
  partial sequences across read boundaries. Decoded codepoints then split into two
  categories: printable text and control information. Control bytes below 0x20, plus escape
  sequences introduced by ESC, drive a state machine — the canonical one being Paul Williams'
  DEC-compatible parser, which recognizes ground state, escape, CSI (ESC [), OSC (ESC ]),
  and DCS states, accumulating parameters and intermediate bytes until a final byte
  dispatches the command. The parser must be robust against garbage: a malformed sequence
  should be discarded and the stream resynchronized, never hang the terminal.

  Printable text goes through width resolution before it lands. This is where most of the
  subtlety lives:
